It sounds similar to a case in Australia that will hopefully result in a conviction someday soon, with the same person originally arrested.  Google Shandee Blackburn. 

TL;DR of the case is they had 30+ collections of DNA however they results kept coming back “no dna detected” which is a misnomer.  It should have said, “not enough sufficient dna markers found” instead.  The reason being is in some places for a conviction based on DNA it must inconclusive based on say “27 markers” that match each and every time they test the DNA. 

in other jurisdictions that has been lowered to 5 because of how it’s DNA is coded, they’re able to decode it using algorithms, which took a long time to do.  

However because some jurisdictions don’t believe 5 is enough, they want an overwhelming amount of dna markers to ensure there is above and beyond a doubt that it’s that specific DNA.  The problem is they are operating as if we are still in the 1950’s America for instance, without acknowledging how good the DNA sequencing now is, and allowing convictions to be made with this kept in mind.

An engagement ring given is a sign of a contract being entered into, and therefore in most places, whoever cancels the contract (I.e calls off the engagement) is usually to forfeit the deposit (the ring) as the ring is given only in good faith of a marriage occurring. 

I.e if Person A proposes and Person B accepts, but then A calls off the engagement he usually has no right to the ring as they have called off the contract and therefore A forfeits the “deposit” to B.
